official_title: Question A. Bond Issue. Affordable Housing Loan. Question A authorizes the City to borrow up to $22,000,000 to be used for the City's Affordable Housing Program. The money may be used to acquire, redevelop, and dispose of property in the City for this purpose, along with related costs. The money may be used to rehabilitate, construct, and operate rental and homeownership developments, including relocation assistance, rental payments, home purchase assistance, housing counseling, project financing, buyer education assistance, activities to support the development of economically diverse housing in the City, and the Affordable Housing Trust Fund. The money may also be used to eliminate unhealthy and unsafe conditions, including blight, and may be used to improve land, buildings, streets, highways, alleys, utilities, and other structures, including all related costs. Voting for this amendment allows the City to borrow this money. Voting against the amendment means the City is not allowed to borrow this money.
plain_summary: Lets the city borrow up to $22 million for its Affordable Housing Program: buying and fixing up property, building or rehabbing homes, helping people with rent, moving or buying a home, and the Affordable Housing Trust Fund.
yes_means: The city may borrow up to $22 million for affordable housing programs.
no_means: The city may not borrow this $22 million for affordable housing.
current_law: Per the ballot itself, the city cannot borrow this money unless voters approve it. Questions A to D are the city's four borrowing requests on this ballot ($280 million combined).
fiscal_impact: Up to $22 million in new city borrowing. The ballot does not state interest or repayment costs.
confusing_wording_note: The ballot text says 'voting for this amendment,' but this is a borrowing (bond) question. It doesn't change the city charter. Questions A through D are all borrowing questions. You'll mark For or Against, not Yes or No.

official_title: Question B. Bond Issue. School Loan. Question B authorizes the City to borrow up to $60,000,000 to be used for school purposes. The money may be used to acquire property in the City for these purposes and to build new or improve existing school buildings, athletic facilities, and community health and recreation facilities, along with all related costs. The money may also be used to acquire equipment for such facilities. Voting for this amendment allows the City to borrow this money. Voting against the amendment means the City is not allowed to borrow this money.
plain_summary: Lets the city borrow up to $60 million to build and fix up school buildings, athletic fields and school health and recreation facilities, and buy equipment for them. The Banner reports most of it would go to heating and air conditioning, windows, doors and fire safety, plus renovations at Edmondson-Westside and Benjamin Franklin high schools.
yes_means: The city may borrow up to $60 million for school buildings and equipment.
no_means: The city may not borrow this $60 million for schools.
current_law: Per the ballot itself, the city cannot borrow this money unless voters approve it.
fiscal_impact: Up to $60 million in new city borrowing. The ballot does not state interest or repayment costs.
confusing_wording_note: The ballot text says 'voting for this amendment,' but this is a borrowing (bond) question. It doesn't change the city charter. You'll mark For or Against.

official_title: Question C. Bond Issue. Community and Economic Development Loan. Question C authorizes the City to borrow up to $50,000,000 to be used for the City's economic development program. The money may be used to acquire, develop, and dispose of property in the City for this purpose, along with related costs. The money may be used to eliminate unhealthy and unsafe conditions, including blight, and to create healthy, sanitary, safe, and green conditions in the City. It may be used to stabilize and improve middle neighborhoods and neighborhood retail corridors, as well as to improve land, buildings, streets, highways, alleys, sidewalks, utilities, parks, recreational land or facilities, and other structures, including all related costs. The money may also be used as loans or grants to develop, improve, or construct buildings in the City for residential or commercial purposes, and as loans or grants for growing businesses, attracting and retaining jobs, encouraging homeownership, providing home repair assistance, promoting economic inclusion, achieving whole-block outcomes, improving the City's cultural life, and promoting City tourism. Voting for this amendment allows the City to borrow this money. Voting against the amendment means the City is not allowed to borrow this money.
plain_summary: Lets the city borrow up to $50 million for economic development: buying and developing property, clearing blight, fixing up shopping streets, sidewalks and parks, and loans or grants for homes, businesses, jobs, home repairs, culture and tourism.
yes_means: The city may borrow up to $50 million for neighborhood and economic development.
no_means: The city may not borrow this $50 million for economic development.
current_law: Per the ballot itself, the city cannot borrow this money unless voters approve it.
fiscal_impact: Up to $50 million in new city borrowing. The ballot does not state interest or repayment costs.
confusing_wording_note: The ballot text says 'voting for this amendment,' but this is a borrowing (bond) question. It doesn't change the city charter. 'Whole-block outcomes' means fixing up a whole block at once rather than one house at a time; the ballot doesn't define it. You'll mark For or Against.

official_title: Question D. Bond Issue. Public Infrastructure Loan. Question D authorizes the City to borrow up to $148,000,000 to be used for the development of public infrastructure owned or controlled by the City. The money may be used to develop buildings owned by the City, the Enoch Pratt Free Library, and public parks and recreational land. It may be used to acquire property in the City and to construct new or improve existing buildings, structures, and auxiliary facilities for use by the City and the Enoch Pratt Free Library. The money may also be used to improve, construct, relocate, or repair buildings, streets, highways, alleys, utilities, and other structures, including information technology infrastructure, as well as to acquire and install trees, equipment, and fixtures, along with all related costs. Voting for this amendment allows the City to borrow this money. Voting against the amendment means the City is not allowed to borrow this money.
plain_summary: Lets the city borrow up to $148 million, the largest of the four borrowing questions, for city buildings, Enoch Pratt library branches, parks and rec centers, streets, utilities, tech systems and trees.
yes_means: The city may borrow up to $148 million for city buildings, libraries, parks and streets.
no_means: The city may not borrow this $148 million for public buildings and infrastructure.
current_law: Per the ballot itself, the city cannot borrow this money unless voters approve it.
fiscal_impact: Up to $148 million in new city borrowing. The ballot does not state interest or repayment costs.
confusing_wording_note: The ballot text says 'voting for this amendment,' but this is a borrowing (bond) question. It doesn't change the city charter. The ballot names no specific projects; The Banner reports planned ones like replacing the Lillian Jones Recreation Center and the William McAbee Pool. You'll mark For or Against.

official_title: Question E. Charter Amendment. Contract Bidding and Awards. Question E amends the City Charter to remove the requirement of awarding a contract to the lowest bidder, removes the process for resolving tie bids, and removes provisions governing the bid bonds and performance bonds required by some contractors. Voting for this Amendment removes these provisions from the Charter, which will become effective November 7, 2028, unless an ordinance or regulation governing the topic is adopted sooner. Voting against the amendment leaves the current Charter language governing contract bidding and awards in place.
plain_summary: Takes the 'lowest bidder' rule out of the city charter, along with the charter's rules on tie bids and on bid and performance bonds (money guarantees some contractors must post). City law or agency rules would set those instead.
yes_means: The lowest-bidder rule and related bond rules come out of the charter, and the city sets contracting rules by ordinance or regulation instead.
no_means: The charter keeps requiring most city contracts to go to the lowest responsive and responsible bidder, along with its tie-bid and bond rules.
current_law: Charter Article VI, Section 11(h) requires the Board of Estimates to award contracts to the 'lowest responsive and responsible bidder' (or, for requests for proposals, the highest-scoring one), sets a tie-bid process, and sets bid-bond and performance-bond rules.
confusing_wording_note: A For vote doesn't write a new contracting rule. It deletes the current one from the charter and leaves the replacement to a future ordinance or regulation. The change kicks in when that replacement is adopted, or on November 7, 2028 at the latest, even if nothing replaces it. 'Responsive and responsible' means the bid meets the job's requirements and the company can do the work. Question F separately removes other contracting duties of the Board of Estimates.

supporters_case.text: Council President Zeke Cohen, who sits on the Board of Estimates, said 'the low bid often does not end up being the lowest bid' because low bidders 'come back or change work orders' the city is locked into. A May 2026 letter from 20 groups, including Clean Water Action, 1199SEIU, Unite Here Local 7, CASA and Progressive Maryland, backed the earlier combined bill, saying the rule means the city 'often gets the cheapest, rather than the best, product.'

opponents_case.text: No organized campaign against Question E was found. When the Council debated the original all-in-one charter bill in April, some members objected to bundling and to weakening public notice; Baltimore Brew reported that critics 'warned they need more study.' The Council then split the bill into separate questions.

official_title: Question F. Charter Amendment. Legislation, Budget, and Board of Estimates. Question F amends the City Charter's legislative process, the annual budget process, and the role of the Board of Estimates. It shortens the amount of time in which the Mayor can veto legislation passed by the City Council and the amount of time the City Council has to override the Mayor's veto. The Amendment also eliminates the preliminary budget hearing process and transfers from the Board of Estimates to the Mayor the responsibility to prepare and submit the proposed budget before April 30 each year. The City Council must then adopt the budget at least eight days before the beginning of the fiscal year on July 1, and any veto and veto override process must be completed by then. The Amendment removes the current $1 million dollar cap on the amount that may be used as a contingent fund for emergencies or other unexpected needs. It allows the Finance Director and the Planning Commission to make new recommendations about the proposed budget after it is submitted to the City Council and allows the City Council to add amounts based on those recommendations before final passage. The Amendment also transfers from the Board of Estimates to the Finance Director or the Planning Commission the authority to make supplemental appropriation recommendations outside of the annual budget process. The Amendment transfers from the Board of Estimates to the Finance Department the responsibility to estimate revenues and formulate the annual rates for all property taxes, and transfers from the Board of Estimates to the Finance Director the responsibility to estimate any surpluses. It also transfers from the Board of Estimates to the Mayor the authority to increase or decrease the salaries of municipal officers in preparing the budget. The Amendment removes from the Charter a number of other duties assigned to the Board of Estimates, including formulating and executing the fiscal policy of the City, advertising for contracts, establishing the process for professional services contracts and for bidder prequalification, approving emergency contracts, fixing salary and wage scales of employees, approving collective bargaining agreements, determining bonds of City officials, establishing procedures for paying or releasing claims against or claims held by the City, fixing the salary of officials in the State's Attorney's Office, and approving expenditures for new improvements. These roles could be given to other agencies or departments by City ordinance. Voting for this amendment brings about the changes described above, with the following effective dates: November 7, 2028, for Charter sections that are removed, unless an ordinance or regulation governing that topic is adopted sooner; December 5, 2028, for changes to approving and vetoing legislation; and December 3, 2026, for all other changes. Voting against the amendment leaves the current Charter language governing legislation, budget, and the Board of Estimates in place.
plain_summary: Rewrites how Baltimore builds its budget. The mayor, not the Board of Estimates, would write the budget and send it to the City Council by April 30. It also changes veto deadlines, lifts the $1 million cap on the emergency fund, and moves many Board of Estimates duties to the mayor, the Finance Department or future city laws.
yes_means: The mayor prepares the budget instead of the Board of Estimates, veto deadlines change, and many Board of Estimates duties move elsewhere.
no_means: The current budget process, veto deadlines and Board of Estimates duties stay in the charter as they are.
current_law: The Board of Estimates (the mayor, the City Council president, the comptroller, and two mayoral appointees, the city solicitor and public works director) prepares the budget, holds preliminary hearings and sends it to the Council at least 45 days before July 1. The mayor has three Council meetings to veto a bill; the Council can reconsider a veto starting 5 days and up to 20 days after the mayor's objections are read. The emergency contingent fund is capped at $1 million.
confusing_wording_note: One question bundles dozens of changes with three start dates: December 3, 2026 for most; December 5, 2028 for veto timing; November 7, 2028 for deleted sections unless replaced sooner. It doesn't change who sits on the Board of Estimates. The ballot says it 'shortens' veto and override windows, while supporters say it gives the Council more time to override a budget veto. Both are true: regular bills get shorter windows, and the budget gets a schedule with room for a veto and override before July 1. Question E, a separate question, removes the charter's lowest-bidder rule for city contracts.

supporters_case.text: A May 2026 letter from 20 Baltimore groups (including Clean Water Action, Progressive Maryland, Jews United for Justice, CASA and the Public Justice Center) urged passage of the earlier combined bill, saying it would give 'the City Council more time to deliberate on the budget, by removing the redundant Board of Estimates step.' Council President Zeke Cohen said this year's changes focus on 'allowing more time for the council to override a mayoral veto.'

opponents_case.text: No organized campaign against Question F was found. In April, Budget Committee chair Danielle McCray called the original package 'reckless' and objected to dropping newspaper contract notices ('We still have seniors that need that information'); by June she voiced no objection. Former Councilman Carl Stokes criticized leaders for putting off a real Board of Estimates overhaul to 2028 instead of doing it now.

official_title: Question G. Charter Amendment. Franchises and Minor Privileges. Question G amends the City Charter language governing how the City allows third parties to use certain City property. It adds the City's stormwater system to the list of City property that cannot be sold or rented out as a franchise. It clarifies that space in the City's conduit system can be rented out as a franchise, but the conduit system itself still cannot be sold. The Amendment also simplifies the general provisions governing franchise agreements and other such grants. The Amendment updates the language for granting minor privileges to use a portion of City property by clarifying the definition of minor privilege, including temporary and permanent varieties, and permitting minor privileges to be further identified and defined by ordinance. It also removes the Board of Estimates' authority to grant minor privileges, along with related processes, and instead allows minor privileges to be granted by an executive agency under a new process to be established by City ordinance. The Amendment also eliminates certain obsolete provisions in the Charter pertaining to street railways and trackless trolleys. Voting for this amendment brings about the changes described above with the following effective dates: November 7, 2028, for Charter sections that are removed, unless an ordinance or regulation governing that topic is adopted sooner; and December 3, 2026, for all other changes. Voting against the amendment leaves the current Charter language governing franchises and minor privileges in place.
plain_summary: Updates the rules for letting others use city property. The stormwater system can't be sold or rented out as a franchise. Space in the city's underground cable conduit can be rented, but the conduit still can't be sold. A city agency, not the Board of Estimates, would approve 'minor privileges' like sidewalk signs or seating.
yes_means: The stormwater system is protected from sale, conduit rules are clarified, and a city agency instead of the Board of Estimates approves minor uses of sidewalks and streets.
no_means: The charter's current rules on franchises and minor privileges stay as they are.
current_law: The charter already bars selling the city's conduit system (approved by voters in 2022) and its water system (2018). The Board of Estimates grants minor privileges today.
confusing_wording_note: The State Board of Elections' web page printed the wrong title for this question ('Legislation, Budget, and Board of Estimates,' which is Question F's title). The certified ballot correctly says 'Franchises and Minor Privileges.' Here a 'franchise' means a long-term right to use city property, not a chain restaurant.

supporters_case.text: This change was split out of the charter package backed by Council President Zeke Cohen. It removes the requirement that the Board of Estimates approve minor privileges, 'requests for structures like sandwich boards or outdoor seating' in the public right-of-way. Baltimore Brew reports the bills were 'pushed as a way to streamline government and improve efficiency.'

official_title: Question H. Charter Amendment. Department of Water and Wastewater. Question H establishes in the City Charter a new Department of Water and Wastewater, which will be supervised and directed by a Director. It transfers from the Department of Public Works to this new Department the responsibility to oversee the City's water supply system and its wastewater system, along with related duties. The Amendment also removes from the Charter the requirement that bureaus within the Department of Public Works must be established or abolished by City ordinance. Voting for this amendment brings about the changes described above, which will become effective January 1, 2029. Voting against the amendment leaves the current Charter language governing water and wastewater systems in place.
plain_summary: Pulls drinking water and sewage out of the Department of Public Works and creates a separate Department of Water and Wastewater with its own director. It takes effect January 1, 2029. It also lets the city reorganize Public Works bureaus without passing a city law each time.
yes_means: Baltimore creates a stand-alone Department of Water and Wastewater starting January 1, 2029.
no_means: Water and sewer stay a bureau inside the Department of Public Works.
current_law: Water and wastewater are run by a bureau inside the Department of Public Works, as they have been for more than 100 years. The system also serves Baltimore County and parts of other counties.
fiscal_impact: No official fiscal estimate found. City officials told The Banner they do not expect costs to rise, and the Public Works director said costs should go down.
confusing_wording_note: Nothing changes until January 1, 2029. The question does not set water or sewer rates. The system serves Baltimore County too, but only city voters decide this.

supporters_case.text: Mayor Brandon Scott, Council President Zeke Cohen and Comptroller Bill Henry jointly backed the split after S&P cut the city wastewater utility's rating from A+ to A- in February 2026. Scott: a stand-alone agency 'is the best way to protect this critical city asset.' A 2024 regional water task force also recommended a separate utility.

official_title: Question I. Charter Amendment. Baltimore Baby Fund. Question I is a charter amendment to create the “Baltimore Baby Fund” as a new, separate fund in City government. The City could use money in the Baby Fund only to enhance the economic stability of families with newborns in Baltimore City. The City could not use money from the Baby Fund to replace funding for newborn children that already exists in this year’s City budget. The amendment would require each year’s City budget to include a contribution to the Baby Fund. The City’s required annual contribution to the Baby Fund will be $0.03 for every $100 in taxable property value in the City. The Baby Fund will also be able to accept grants and donations. Money in the Baby Fund will stay in the Baby Fund until the City spends it for the benefit of families with newborns. The City could not transfer money in the Baby Fund to any other purpose. Voting for this amendment would create the Baltimore Baby Fund and require the City to fund it as described above. Voting against this amendment would mean that the Baltimore Baby Fund would not be created.
plain_summary: Creates a Baltimore Baby Fund in the city charter to help families with newborns. Each year the city budget must put in at least 3 cents for every $100 of property value in the city (The Banner projects about $15 million). The mayor and City Council would decide later how the money is given out.
yes_means: Baltimore creates the Baby Fund and must put money into it every year for families with newborns.
no_means: No Baby Fund is created, and the city is not required to set this money aside.
current_law: No such fund exists. The city ran a guaranteed-income pilot for young parents from 2022 to 2024. A 2024 'baby bonus' version ($1,000 per baby) was kept off the ballot after the Supreme Court of Maryland ruled it was not proper charter material.
fiscal_impact: A required yearly set-aside of at least $0.03 per $100 of assessed property value; The Banner projects about $15 million a year. No official fiscal note found.
confusing_wording_note: Watch the letter: this is Question I (the letter i). It sits on the same ballot as statewide Question 1 (the number one, about state worker contracts), and even a TV station called it 'Question 1.' The '$0.03 for every $100' line reads like a new property tax, but it sets no tax rate; it requires the city to set aside that amount from its budget each year. The full charter text says 'at least' that amount, so the city could put in more. The fund can't replace newborn spending already in the city's fiscal 2027 budget.

supporters_case.text: Backed by the Baltimore Baby Fund campaign (petition led by Nate Golden of the Maryland Child Alliance) and Mayor Brandon Scott, who in a joint statement described it as 'a natural evolution' of his guaranteed-income pilot for young parents. Golden: 'the research shows that if we can get direct resources into the hands of parents, it can really be an important use of the funds.'

opponents_case.text: No organized campaign against the 2026 version was found. In 2024 Mayor Scott fought to keep the earlier 'baby bonus' version off the ballot, and the Supreme Court of Maryland agreed it 'wasn't proper charter material.' The 2026 version was rewritten to leave the details to the mayor and Council.
